briefs.label: Morning Brief
briefs.title: New Doors Open in A2 While Lansing Weighs Tax Relief; DEA Inches Toward Schedule III as Psychedelics Hit Warp Speed
briefs.top: Ann Arbor got a brand-new dispensary this weekend and Upper Peninsula operators are proving the 24% wholesale tax can be managed, not just survived, while a repeal bill and a September court trial keep real relief on the table. Nationally, the DEA is now on record arguing cannabis doesn't belong in Schedule I anymore, and the FDA just handed three psychedelic drug developers a fast lane that could put the first-ever approved psilocybin therapy on shelves within months.

local.text: New Standard opened its Ann Arbor location over Labor Day weekend with giveaways and discounts running Sept. 3-6, adding fresh retail energy and foot traffic to one of the state's most competitive dispensary markets.

In Muskegon, Fields Cannary is targeting a fall opening for a fully integrated cannabis hospitality concept combining retail, on-site consumption, dining, and event licensing under one roof — the kind of format bet operators statewide are watching closely.

While tax pressure has forced closures elsewhere in the U.P., Rize has kept growing across its three locations by negotiating cost-sharing arrangements with suppliers that split the 24% wholesale tax burden instead of absorbing it alone — a playbook other operators are starting to copy.

A Republican state representative has introduced House Bill 6224 to repeal the 24% wholesale tax outright, and the Michigan Cannabis Industry Association's constitutional challenge is now heading toward a September 2026 trial — the biggest variable that could finally move pricing in operators' favor.

The hard number: the wholesale tax generated just $37.38 million in Q2, badly missing projections, and Higher Love closed five of its nine U.P. stores citing the levy — pressure that's fueling the repeal push and giving MiCIA's lawsuit added political weight heading into its court date.

national.text: The DEA formally argued in its final post-hearing brief that marijuana no longer meets the statutory criteria for Schedule I and should move to Schedule III — the clearest federal signal yet that rescheduling is advancing, with a judge's recommendation now the next milestone to watch.

The FDA issued Commissioner's National Priority Vouchers to Compass Pathways (psilocybin for treatment-resistant depression), Usona Institute (psilocybin for major depressive disorder), and Transcend Therapeutics (methylone for PTSD) — vouchers that compress FDA review from roughly a year down to one to two months.

Compass Pathways' COMP360 hit its primary endpoint in a second Phase 3 trial for treatment-resistant depression, making it the first classic psychedelic to consistently post statistically significant, clinically meaningful results — the company is targeting a completed NDA submission and commercial readiness by Q4 2026.

The FDA finalized new psychedelic trial guidance addressing the functional-unblinding problem that sank Lykos' 2024 MDMA rejection, formally codifying active placebos and blinding controls sponsors must use — clearing a path for MDMA-assisted therapy to come back around, alongside a public FDA hearing on psychedelic therapeutics set for September 14.

M&A is consolidating around stronger players even as weaker ones stumble: Vireo Growth completed its acquisition of 17 PharmaCann Colorado dispensaries for roughly $49 million, and Grown Rogue is picking up PharmaCann's New York cultivation and retail assets — expansion moves happening alongside distress at smaller operators like Justice Grown, which is now in loan default.
